passages.t: Here shall be the house of the LORD
passages.happening:
David says, “Here shall be the house of the LORD God, as well as the altar of burnt offering for Israel” (verse 1). He gathers the foreigners living in the land and sets stonecutters among them to prepare finished stone (verse 2). He provides iron for nails and fittings, ‘more bronze than could be weighed’ (verse 3), and cedar beyond counting from Sidon and Tyre (verse 4).

David says that Solomon is young and inexperienced, and that the house must be ‘famous and glorious throughout all lands’ (verse 5). ‘So David made lavish preparations before his death’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 21 ended at the altar on Ornan's threshing floor, and this chapter opens with David naming the place. From here to the end of 1 Chronicles the story turns entirely to the temple. David may not build it, as God said in chapter 17, but the Chronicler shows him doing everything short of building: gathering materials, organizing workers, charging his son and enlisting the leaders. The temple will be Solomon's building, but in Chronicles it is David's vision.

First Kings has Solomon making the preparations, with little about David's part. Chronicles gives David a large share. That emphasis suited the Chronicler's first readers, who worshiped in the rebuilt second temple, completed around 516 or 515 BC. By tracing its worship back to David, he gave their modest temple a place in the promise to David.

The foreigners set to cutting stone were non-Israelite residents of the land, put to forced labor; Solomon later counted and assigned them in the same way. Sidon and Tyre, the great Phoenician cities, supplied the cedar, continuing the friendship with Hiram from chapter 14. The verb for prepare, kun, runs through the chapter, and it is the same verb used of God establishing David's throne: David prepares a house for God while God establishes a house for David.
passages.later: Second Chronicles says, ‘Solomon numbered all the foreign men in the land of Israel following the census his father David had conducted’ (2 Chronicles 2:17). First Kings says that ‘Solomon had 70,000 porters and 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains’ (1 Kings 5:15).
passages.asks: David could not build the house, so he prepared everything he could for the one who would. Ask what work you are preparing that someone else will finish. And ask whether you can give yourself to it without needing your name on it.

passages.happening:
David calls Solomon and tells him to build the house for the LORD (verse 6). He had wanted to build it himself, but God said, ‘You have shed much blood and waged great wars’ (verse 8). God promised instead ‘a son will be born to you who will be a man of rest’ (verse 9), whose name will be Solomon, a son who will build the house and whose throne will be established forever (verses 9-10).

‘Now, my son, may the LORD be with you, and may you succeed in building the house of the LORD your God, as He said you would’ (verse 11). David prays for insight for him so that he will keep the law, and says, ‘Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged’ (verse 13). He lists what he has gathered, 100,000 talents of gold and 1,000,000 talents of silver among it, and the craftsmen ready, and ends, ‘Now begin the work, and may the LORD be with you’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The charge retells God's promise from chapter 17 with new details: why David may not build, what Solomon's name means, and the promise of rest and peace. The name Solomon, Shelomoh, sounds like shalom, peace, and verse 9 plays on it. Shalom is more than the absence of war; it is things as they should be. Rest, menuchah, means security from enemies in the land God gave, a theme running through Deuteronomy and Joshua. The king of rest, not the warrior king, builds the house of God. First Kings gives the reason from another side, as the hard question below says.

Be strong and courageous is the formula of handing over leadership in Israel's story. Moses said it to Joshua, and so did God. Using it here casts Solomon as a new Joshua, completing what his predecessor began and bringing Israel into rest.

The quantities in verse 14 are immense. With a talent commonly estimated at around thirty kilograms, the gold alone would weigh about three thousand metric tons, far beyond what any ancient kingdom is known to have held. Interpreters handle this in different ways: as royal overstatement of a kind common in ancient inscriptions, as a copying problem with numbers, or as a unit different from the one usually assumed. The Chronicler's point is plain either way: David gave more than could be weighed or counted.
passages.later: Moses said to Joshua before all Israel, “Be strong and courageous, for you will go with this people into the land that the LORD swore to their fathers to give them” (Deuteronomy 31:7). First Kings gives Solomon's reason as ‘the wars waged on all sides against my father David’ (1 Kings 5:3).
passages.hard:
Why was David's bloodshed a reason he could not build the temple, when his victories came from God?

The chapters before say twice that the LORD gave David his victories, and yet here the blood he shed keeps him from building. The Bible gives more than one side of the refusal. Second Samuel 7 grounds it simply in God's will. First Kings says that wars on every side kept David from building until his enemies were subdued. Chronicles names the blood itself. Many read the last two as complementing each other: both explain why the son, and not the father, built the house.

The Chronicler sets the reason beside the son's name. The house where God's name dwells is built by a man of rest, and the warrior king prepares for it. The Bible records David's wars as part of how God kept his promise, and it also refuses to make David a model in every act. The chapter does not condemn David; it gives him the work of preparing. But it does not call his wars holy either.
passages.asks: David told his son to be strong and courageous, and not to be afraid. Ask who needs to hear those words from you, and whether you have said them. And ask what you have been afraid to begin.

passages.t: Set your heart to seek the LORD
passages.happening: David orders all the leaders of Israel to help Solomon (verse 17). ‘Is not the LORD your God with you, and has He not granted you rest on every side?’ (verse 18). ‘Now set your heart and soul to seek the LORD your God. Get started building the sanctuary of the LORD God’ (verse 19), so that the ark and the holy articles can be brought into the house built for the LORD's name.
passages.hearers:
The private charge to Solomon becomes a public charge to the leaders. The order matters. Before they build, they are to seek the LORD with heart and soul. Seeking, darash, is the word on which Saul was judged in chapter 10 and which David failed to do the first time he moved the ark. The temple is not a building project first; it is the fruit of a people seeking God.

The goal is to bring the ark and the holy things into the house. The ark that was neglected in Saul's days, carried the wrong way in chapter 13 and brought up rightly in chapter 15, is to find its resting place.
passages.later: Moses had said, ‘But if from there you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul’ (Deuteronomy 4:29).
passages.asks: David told the leaders to seek God before they began to build. Ask whether your plans for God's work begin with seeking God. And ask what it would mean for you to set your heart and soul on it this week.
